pageCache.text:
Welcome to
Staverton Primary School
At Staverton, we are proud to be a small school with a big heart. In a world where many schools are part of large trusts, our individuality and close-knit community set us apart. Here, every child is known, valued, and encouraged to achieve their very best.We are especially delighted that Ofsted has recognised our Early Years provision as Outstanding– giving children the strongest possible start to their learning journey.Our vision is symbolised in the beautiful tree mural at the heart of our school: a life-giving tree filled with unique birds, each one celebrated. Staverton is a place where children truly belong, flourish, and develop a love of learning that lasts a lifetime.At Staverton, every day is an open day. We warmly invite you to explore our website, read what our families say, and most importantly, come and visit us in person. You’ll find a school community that is welcoming, inspiring, and full of life.

pageCache.pageTitle: Headteacher's Welcome | Staverton C of E Primary School
pageCache.text:
Headteacher’s welcome
At Staverton Primary School, we believe education is about far more than results. It’s about belonging, curiosity, creativity and character. We are a small school with a big heart, serving our village and surrounding area with pride.
While many schools today are part of large multi-academy trusts, Staverton remains rooted in its own individuality. Our strength comes from our close-knit community: staff who go the extra mile, families who work in partnership, and children who are known, valued and celebrated as unique individuals.
The best way to understand what makes Staverton special is to experience it for yourself. Whether you are a prospective parent, a neighbour, or a visitor to the area, we warmly invite you to come and see our school in action.
Edward Powe, Headteacher
Our vision: A life-giving tree
Why families choose Staverton
Outstanding Early Years
Our Outstanding Early Years OFSTED rating reflects the exceptional start our youngest learners receive.
A school without walls
Our curriculum is broad, balanced and exciting – designed to prepare children for the world beyond school.
A love of books
We believe reading is the greatest gift we can give our children. That’s why it is woven into everything we do.
In our families' own words

pageCache.pageTitle: Collective Worship | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Collective worship
At Staverton the children take part in a daily act of collective worship (also known as an assembly). As a church school, this is a requirement of the school to have a daily act of collective worship, but more importantly, it is a time within our busy school day, where we can come together and learn about important values for our lives.
Our aims
Through collective worship, we hope to:
Express praise and thanksgiving to God
Be still and reflect
Foster respect and deepen spiritual awareness
Affirm Christian values and attitudes
Share each other's joys and challenges
Celebrate special times in the Christian calendar
Express praise and thanksgiving to God
Be still and reflect
Foster respect and deepen spiritual awareness
Affirm Christian values and attitudes
Share each other's joys and challenges
Celebrate special times in the Christian calendar
School prayers
May the Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with us all, ever more. Amen.
The Peace of the Lord be always with you. (And also with you.)
May the Lord bless you and keep you. May the Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you. May the Lord turn his face towards you, and bring you peace.
Our pattern of worship
Our collective worship is centred around a weekly theme, linked to the term’s value or an event in the calendar. Each day offers children a different way to take part:
Every collective worship includes reminders of our vision and values, a moment of reflection through stillness or prayer, a chance to respond to the theme, and an opportunity to engage spiritually through music. We also explore our values through storytelling – a picture book, an orally told story or drama – and every session includes some interaction, so children take part in worship rather than just observing it.
Each collective worship begins with the same gathering phrase – “Peace be with you” – and the children respond, “and also with you.” It’s the same exchange as in The Peace, above, and is a piece of Anglican worship children hear and join in with every day, not just something they learn about.
Whole-school collective worship, introducing the week’s theme
Whole-school celebration assembly
Is collective worship compulsory?
Staverton is a voluntary-controlled Church of England school, maintained by Wiltshire local education authority, and we welcome children from families of all faiths and none. Our Christian vision and values shape everything we do – in assembly, in lessons, in play, and in how we treat each other. We do not offer a separate religious assembly for other faiths.
Daily worship informs many aspects of life at our school, so while any pupil or member of staff is entitled to withdraw from assembly, doing so means missing an important part of school life. We want families to make that decision with full information, not in the dark
It's worth knowing that collective worship is not a church service or religious ceremony. Anyone taking part is simply invited to join in with whatever they feel comfortable with – that might be a prayer, a reading, or a song – and much of what we do is simply a celebration of school life, achievements and news, alongside the reflective and spiritual elements.
If you would like to withdraw your child from the religious aspects of assembly, please get in touch with the Headteacher, who will be glad to talk through what this means in practice. Staff who would prefer not to take part in the religious aspects of assembly are also welcome to speak with the Headteacher directly.

pageCache.pageTitle: Our Vision & Values | Staverton C of E Primary School
pageCache.text:
Our vision, values and ethos
We believe that our school is like that tree, which grows over time as wide as we can with branches that reach out into our community, providing shade, shelter and life for Staverton. The tree is home to the children, parents, staff and community members, who are like the birds nesting within its branches. They are nurtured in our school, and in time flourish, developing skills, attitudes and values which are important for adult life.
Our vision
Our vision is based on Jesus’ parable of the mustard seed, which describes the Kingdom of Heaven growing and flourishing from small, humble beginnings.
This parable is a powerful reminder that incredible things come from the humblest of beginnings but it also illustrates the abundant life-giving nature of God’s kingdom for all who seek it.
We place importance on every child belonging to our school and encourage the children to show their uniqueness, every child has a unique song to sing. By the end of their time at Staverton, they will be able to spread their wings and fly high.
Staverton provides a deep and rich education that encompasses not only academic knowledge and skills, but also teach spiritual, moral, social and cultural learning. Throughout a child’s journey through school, they will be taught key values, rooted in Christian distinctiveness.
Courage
Forgiveness
Hope
Kindness
Respect
Trust
How our values come to life
Our values aren't just something we talk about – they show up in everyday school life, in ways like these:
High-quality literature embedded throughout the curriculum
Charity fundraising events, chosen by the children
In our families' own words
Living our vision
Our ethos
If Staverton is to reflect the idea of being a life-giving tree, it's worth asking what that actually looks like in practice. It's not something easily captured in a sentence, and it looks different depending on the situation – it calls for constant reflection, not a rehearsed set of buzzwords. The real question is simply: how should we be?
We've summarised our ethos below:
Children and adults should be open, honest and vulnerable, knowing they are accepted for who they are, and that God turns our weaknesses into his opportunities. There should be open lines of communication between parents, the wider community and the school. Those who belong to Staverton should feel safe, and therefore able to be themselves.
We shouldn't put a limit on what we expect from people, and we should encourage everyone to reach their full potential and beyond. This means children and adults alike should be challenged in their learning, moving from good to great.
Theological foundations
The image of God's kingdom as a life-giving tree (arbor vitae) runs through many passages of scripture. In John's Gospel, Jesus describes himself as the vine, providing nourishment to the branches, without whom no fruit can grow. The psalmist David describes those who meditate on God's word as being like "trees planted in streams of water, who produce fruit in season and whose leaves do not wither."
Regardless of religious upbringing or belief, the image of Staverton as a life-giving tree has a universal appeal, woven into countless cultures and traditions. The same is true of birds – children and adults alike can identify with birds as a symbol of freedom, aspiration and joy.
Living by this vision isn't easy. It asks the school to be counter-cultural: to be accepting of everyone in a world quick to judge, and to offer help and support even where it would be easier not to.

pageCache.pageTitle: Welcome to Nestlings | Staverton C of E Primary School
pageCache.text:
Welcome to Nestlings Nursery
Nestlings is where your child's Staverton journey begins – a warm, nurturing space where they'll build friendships, discover a love of stories, and grow in confidence, right through to their first day in Reception.
Nestlings children can join our wrap-around care alongside school-age children, from as early as 7:45am through to 5:15pm – giving working families flexible, continuous care delivered by the same trusted team throughout the day.
Every member of our Nestlings team is appropriately qualified and DBS-checked, and follows the same safeguarding standards as the rest of Staverton – so your child is cared for by people who know them, in a setting that takes their safety as seriously as their learning.
What makes Nestlings special
A love of reading, from day one
Storytelling and books are woven into everyday life at Nestlings. From regular library visits to daily story time, we want every child to fall in love with books long before they can read them for themselves.
Learning through play
Children learn best when they're curious, active, and having fun. Our play-based approach lets children explore, choose, and lead their own learning, with our team on hand to guide, extend, and join in.
Emotional wellbeing at the heart of everything
We take time to build genuine relationships with every child, so they feel safe, known, and confident enough to be themselves. A strong sense of belonging is the foundation everything else is built on.
A seamless step into school
Nestlings isn't separate from Staverton – it's the start of it. Children move into our Reception class already familiar with our staff, our building, and our values, making that first step into "big school" feel natural rather than daunting.
Our values
Nestlings shares the same values as the rest of Staverton School: Courage, Kindness, Respect, Forgiveness, Trust, and Hope. These aren't just words on a wall – they shape how our team speaks to children, how children are encouraged to treat one another, and how we build a community where every family feels welcome from their very first visit.
Living these values out from age 2 means children arrive in Reception already familiar with the language and spirit of Staverton life, rather than encountering it for the first time on their first day of school.
Our approach to learning
At Nestlings, we believe young children learn best when they're an active participant in their own learning, not a passive recipient of it. Our child-centred, play-based approach follows each child's interests and curiosity, giving them the freedom to explore, make choices, and take the lead – with our team gently guiding, extending, and joining in along the way.
We're just as committed to building independence as we are to academic foundations. Children are encouraged to try things for themselves, make their own decisions, and problem-solve – building the confidence and resilience that will serve them well throughout their time at Staverton and beyond.
We're proud to be a welcoming, inclusive community where every family feels they belong, regardless of background or circumstance. It's this sense of belonging, combined with genuinely exciting, hands-on learning, that means children arrive at Nestlings each day happy and excited to be there.

pageCache.pageTitle: Modern Foreign Languages | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Modern foreign languages
At Staverton, we help children respond to speakers of French, building a greater understanding of French-speaking communities – their cultural traditions and aspects of daily life.
Our approach
Building confidence
Children use their knowledge of grammatical structures to write at varying length and speak with increasing confidence, fluency and spontaneity.
Songs, rhymes and vocabulary
Children explore the patterns and sounds of language through songs and rhymes, and broaden their vocabulary and their ability to understand new words.
This is what it means to be a linguist at Staverton

pageCache.pageTitle: Music | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Music
At Staverton, we develop children’s understanding and experience of music, inspiring their curiosity about musical expression and creativity.
Our approach
All children attend a regular music assembly, where they listen attentively to a piece chosen from the Model Music Curriculum’s suggested list. They’re taught a variety of songs, both for performance at school events and simply for the joy of singing.
All children have the opportunity to perform during our Harvest Service, Christmas Carol Service and leavers’ performances, sharing their music in school and at local care homes and churches. Parents, carers and members of our wider school community are invited to join us.
Building on musical history
Teachers use BBC Ten Pieces as the basis for developing children's understanding of musical history, knowledge and skills.
Visiting musicians
‍Each year, the school welcomes musicians to perform for the children – sharing their journey into music and teaching about their instrument.
Whole-class instrument lessons
All children in Key Stage 2 have whole-class instrument lessons as part of their music curriculum: recorder or glockenspiel in Years 3 and 4, and ukulele in Years 5 and 6.
This is what it means to be a musician at Staverton

pageCache.pageTitle: School Governors | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
School governors
The governors of Staverton C of E Primary School work with the Headteacher and senior leadership team to set the school's strategic direction. Our role is to ensure every child receives the very best education we can provide – the best possible outcome for every child is our ultimate goal. We're not involved in the school's day-to-day operation. Instead, we set the criteria by which the school is managed, and both support and challenge the Headteacher and senior staff to ensure the school performs as well as it should, and that every pupil has the best opportunity to learn and develop.
Our governors
Governor activity
We meet as a full governing body each term. Alongside these meetings, we monitor progress against the School Development Plan and build strong links with subject leaders through regular visits to the school.
We also fulfil our statutory obligations, overseeing safeguarding and special educational needs provision, monitoring attendance, the Early Years Foundation Stage, Health and Safety, and the school's financial position, including public funds paid through the Pupil and Sports Premiums. Governors also monitor suspensions, complaints and any incidents of whistleblowing.
Our governing body is made up of 5 parent governors (elected by their peers), 2 foundation governors (appointed by the Diocese), 1 local authority governor, 2 staff governors and 5 co-opted governors (appointed by the governing body). It's a voluntary role, and one that plays a vital part in the life of a successful school. The normal term of office is four years. After that, any governor who wishes to continue can stand for a further term, and – provided no one else has come forward for the position – will typically be re-elected or reconfirmed in their role.
We recognise and appreciate that governors bring different areas of expertise to the governing body.
Who sits on our governing body
Foundation governors
Appointed by the Diocesan Board of Education to secure the school's religious character, and to ensure that character is preserved and developed.
Parent governors
Any parent or primary carer of a pupil at the school can stand for election when a parent governor position becomes vacant. If more than one parent expresses interest, an election is held in which all parents can vote. Parent governors don't formally represent parents on the governing body, but act as a link between parents and governors, keeping in touch with parents' views.
Co-opted governors
Appointed by the governing body for having skills judged to contribute to effective governance and the school's success.
Staff governors
A member of school staff, elected by their fellow staff.
Local authority governors
Appointed by the local education authority. As a team, we come from very different backgrounds, and we're always looking for fresh faces to join us. If you'd like to know more, please contact the school office and one of us will get in touch.

Art
At Staverton, we believe every child is a natural artist. Through Art, children explore ideas, techniques and materials to express themselves, respond to the world around them, and develop a lifelong appreciation for creativity in all its forms.
Our approach
Knowledge of artists and techniques
Pupils are equipped with knowledge of a variety of artists, craft makers and designers – knowledge they use to create their own outcomes, exploring and recording ideas through a range of media.
Annual projects
‍Every year, children complete projects in drawing, painting and sculpture, focusing on techniques including line, shape, colour, space and texture. Children create art galleries to share their work with the wider school community.
Art Week and visiting artists
Children take part in an Art Week each year, creating artwork based on a chosen theme or topic. Staverton also regularly welcomes inspirational artists into school to create artwork, run workshops, and hold showcases.
This is what it means to be an artist at Staverton School

pageCache.pageTitle: Computing | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Computing
In Computing, we develop children's understanding of information technology, computer science and digital literacy, and their role in a global world.
Our approach
What we cover
‍Children take part in a range of activities covering IT (using technology), computer science (understanding coding and programming), and digital literacy (how to behave safely and responsibly online).
Plugged and unplugged learning
‍Some activities are "unplugged," meaning they don't require any technology at all, while others make use of technology, including iPads and the school's Chromebooks.
Purple Mash and Safer Internet Day
We use the Purple Mash scheme of work to support our delivery of the computing curriculum. As a whole school, we celebrate Safer Internet Day every year.
This is what it means to be a confident, safe user of technology at Staverton

Geography
Geography at Staverton develops children's understanding, experience and curiosity of the wider world.
Our approach
Understanding our world
Teaching equips pupils with knowledge about diverse places, people, resources, and natural and human environments, alongside a deep understanding of the Earth's key physical and human processes.
Skills that connect and explain
Geographical knowledge, understanding and skills give children the framework to explain how the Earth's features at different scales are shaped, interconnected, and change over time.
Geographical language
Children learn and use technical geographical terminology in appropriate contexts, making links between what they study and the world around them.
This is what it means to be a geographer at Staverton

pageCache.pageTitle: History | Staverton C of E Primary

History
In history at Staverton, we develop children’s understanding and experience of the past, both local and international, sparking their curiosity about the wider world and allowing them to construct narratives to interpret it.
Our approach
Coherent knowledge of the past
‍Pupils gain a coherent knowledge of Britain's past, contextualised within an understanding of the wider world, and develop the skills needed to investigate and draw conclusions about historical periods or events.
Cross-curricular connections
History is firmly embedded within cross-curricular learning. In both Key Stage 1 and 2, history topics are drawn from whole-class texts studied in English – for example, Year 5/6 study the Second World War alongside reading Letters from the Lighthouse by Emma Carroll.
Trips and workshops
‍A variety of workshops and visits take place throughout the year, including themed History days and trips to the SS Great Britain, a Victorian School experience, and the Bovington Tank Museum.
This is what it means to be a historian at Staverton

pageCache.pageTitle: Mathematics | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Mathematics
We use mathematics every day: from telling the time to handling money to reading timetables and so much more. It is vital to be numerate to participate fully in our community and in our world. Therefore, at Staverton we aim to make sure every child has a rich and meaningful maths education.
Our approach
Children learn in a positive environment where it’s safe to take risks and learn from mistakes, building independence of thought, action and problem solving.
We want them to develop a deep understanding of mathematical skills and knowledge they can use to explore, interpret, predict and explain the world, and we create opportunities to apply maths across the curriculum so it feels meaningful and inspires creative thinking.
Fluency
Children become fluent in the fundamentals of maths through varied and frequent practice, developing a conceptual understanding and the ability to recall and apply knowledge rapidly and accurately.
Reasoning
Children explain, justify, question and prove their thinking, exploring patterns, following lines of enquiry, describing relationships and making generalisations. Correct mathematical vocabulary and stem sentences are used in every key stage, giving children the language to talk about maths with confidence.
Problem solving
Children are confident problem solvers, able to apply maths efficiently to a variety of problems and to think logically and systematically.
Maths in the classroom
Our schemes of learning
We use the Maths No Problem scheme for our maths curriculum. It gives children the chance to explore maths and build their skills through a mastery approach, working with concrete, pictorial and abstract ideas and problems.
Lessons follow a clear structure: children explore a problem independently, are taught new skills, practise them through guided learning, and then work independently.
Where possible, classes are taught as single year groups for maths. In year groups where the cohort is larger, children are taught in mixed classes but continue to receive teaching specific to their year group.
Mastering Number at Staverton
Our Foundation Stage and Key Stage 1 classes take part in Mastering Number sessions daily. This is a scheme provided by the National Centre for Excellence in the Teaching of Mathematics (NCETM), which aims to secure firm foundations in the development of good number sense for all children from Reception through to Year 1 and Year 2. The aim over time is that children will leave KS1 with fluency in calculation and a confidence and flexibility with number. Attention is given to the key knowledge and understanding needed in Reception classes, and progression through KS1 to support success in the future.
Our Foundation Stage pupils and parents also take part in a Parental Engagement project linked to Mastering Number. It gives parents skills and resources to help their children continue their learning at home through games and mini activities.

PSHE
Personal, social, health and economic (PSHE) education is an important and necessary part of every child's education at Staverton. Alongside academic learning, PSHE addresses children's wellbeing needs and teaches them skills they can use in their everyday lives.
Our approach
Our scheme
We use the SCARF scheme for PSHE, built around six key themes: Me and My Relationships; Valuing Difference (including a focus on anti-bullying); Keeping Safe; Rights and Respect; Being My Best; and Growing and Changing (our relationships and sex education, or RSE, focus). Our RSE policy is available on our Policies page.
National initiatives
Anti-bullying and safer internet use are also taught at key points in the year, linked to national initiatives, including Safer Internet Day.

pageCache.pageTitle: Reading | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Reading
At Staverton, we want every child to become a confident, capable reader who enjoys books and develops a lifelong love of reading.
Our approach
In Key Stage 2, our carefully chosen reading spine introduces children to a wide range of authors, genres, characters, cultures and experiences. Across the school, we make time to share books simply for the pleasure of listening to and enjoying a story, and children can choose fiction or non-fiction books to read independently or enjoy with an adult. Above all, we want every child to know that books are for everyone, and that there is always another wonderful book waiting to be discovered.
Reading at home
Once children have completed Read Write Inc Phonics (see below), they choose books from our Mini Library to take home that are appropriate for their reading ability while still providing a suitable level of challenge.
Working together
Reading develops most successfully when school and home work together. Regular reading at home, sharing stories, talking about books, and visiting libraries all help children become stronger and more enthusiastic readers.‍
What reading looks like
Once children have completed Read Write Inc Phonics, they take part in a daily reading lesson of at least 30 minutes. Children experience a carefully chosen range of high-quality fiction and non-fiction texts, including a core class book each term.
During reading lessons, children often hear their teacher read aloud fluently and expressively while following along with their own copy of the text. This means all children can enjoy and learn from ambitious books, even when they're not yet able to read them independently.
A key part of reading at Staverton is talking about books. Children are encouraged to share their ideas, listen carefully to others, and use evidence from the text to explain their thinking.

pageCache.pageTitle: Religious Education | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Religious education
Religious education (RE) is the study of world religions and beliefs. It's an essential part of a broad and balanced curriculum, supporting children's spiritual, moral, social and cultural development – helping them explore the deep meaning people find in their experiences, and how this gives purpose to their lives.
Our approach
We want children to leave Staverton holding that same respect for other faiths – understanding how religion shapes individuals, families, communities and cultures, and exploring the political and social impact of religion alongside questions of justice, truth and the meaning of life.
You can read our RE policy, including information about your right to withdraw your child from RE lessons, on our Policies page.
Understanding Christianity
Roughly half of our RE units focus on Christianity, taught through the Understanding Christianity scheme, which explores key themes from the Bible’s story: Creation, People of God, Incarnation, Gospel, Salvation and Kingdom of God. Each unit starts with the text and key story, explores its impact on Christian lives today, then invites children to reflect on their own views.
Exploring other faiths
Our remaining units explore other world views. In Key Stage 1, children study Islam and Judaism; in Key Stage 2, they also study Sikhism, Hinduism, Buddhism and Humanism, including agnostic and atheist world views. Units follow the Emmanuel Project’s enquiry cycle: Engaging, Enquiring, Exploring, Evaluating and Expressing.

pageCache.pageTitle: Science | Staverton C of E Primary
pageCache.text:
Science
Science at Staverton equips children with the knowledge, methods, processes and uses of science that will enable them to understand the physical and natural world around them.
Our approach
Scientific knowledge is embedded through systematic, open-ended enquiry – creatively and rigorously planned, carried out and recorded – so children experience science as something they do, not just something they’re told. Creative, hands-on teaching ignites their curiosity and gives them the ability to explain scientific concepts, opening their minds to the world around them.
Scientific literacy and vocabulary
Understanding scientific concepts depends on scientific literacy, so scientific vocabulary is taught explicitly and used confidently by every member of staff, giving children the language to explain what they discover.
Real-world context
A range of trips and workshops take place across the year groups to help cement knowledge and put science into a real-world context, beyond the classroom.
Scientists who shaped our world
Pupils learn about the contribution scientists have made to understanding and shaping the world we live in – inspiring them to become the next generation of scientific thinkers, and to develop as resilient, creative problem solvers.
How science builds across the school
Our science knowledge progression
Our full Science Knowledge Progression Document sets out exactly what children know and understand as scientists in every topic, at every stage – from identifying common plants in Year 1, to explaining the mechanics of circuits in Year 6. It covers all twelve areas of the science curriculum: plants, living things and their habitats, animals including humans, evolution and inheritance, seasonal changes, materials, rocks, light, forces, sound, electricity, and Earth and space.
Our working scientifically progression
Alongside subject knowledge, children build the skills of working scientifically – asking good questions, making accurate observations and measurements, setting up fair tests, recording and presenting evidence, and drawing sound conclusions. Our Working Scientifically Progression Document sets out how these skills develop from Key Stage 1 through to Years 5 and 6, as children move from answering questions posed by their teacher to independently planning their own scientific enquiries and justifying their choices.

Welcome to Woodpeckers class! We are an energetic, enthusiastic and friendly Year 3/4 class who love learning together. We especially enjoy keeping active, whether that’s through brain breaks, movement games, PE or getting outside.
Woodpeckers
Welcome to Woodpeckers class! We are an energetic, enthusiastic and friendly Year 3/4 class who love learning together. We especially enjoy keeping active, whether that’s through brain breaks, movement games, PE or getting outside.
In our Year 3/4 class, we follow the National Curriculum for Key Stage 2, providing children with a broad and balanced range of learning experiences. We encourage children to become confident, independent and curious learners, with lots of opportunities to learn through practical activities, discussion, teamwork and being active.
A key focus in Year 3/4 is developing secure times table knowledge, with regular practice and fun activities to help children build speed and confidence in preparation for the Year 4 Multiplication Tables Check. We also place a strong emphasis on reading for pleasure, encouraging children to discover new authors, explore different genres and develop a love of books.
Class information
The Firework Maker’s Daughter
Me and My Relationships
The children will bring home a reading book and record to aid their development. Please make sure their folder is brought to school every day.
What we're learning this term
Art
In art this term, we will be learning about different sketching techniques. We will use them in our final piece, drawing a portrait of our favourite authors.
Computing
We will have a weekly computing lesson on animation. We will be following a unit of work from Purple Mash. The children can access Purple Mash at home if they wish.
English
In English this term, The Wolves in the Walls by Neil Gaiman will inspire our own stories, then a report about another tiny creature living in walls. We are focusing on accuracy in spelling, handwriting and punctuation, with Read Write Inc phonics or spelling groups and spellings to practise.
Mathematics
Years 3 and 4 will be exploring multiplication and division this term, with Year 3 starting by subtracting with renaming and Year 4 starting with word problems. Children have a daily times tables lesson, and we ask them to spend 5–10 minutes daily on Times Tables Rock Stars and NumBots.
PE
This term, we will be focusing on social skills within our PE sessions using Real PE. This will include encouraging others, showing and telling others about our ideas, and organising roles and responsibilities.
PSHE
Every term, we will start with a PSHE unit. We will be following the SCARF scheme of work. Our first unit is called ‘Me and My Relationships’.
RE
In RE, children will continue to learn about Hinduism this term. We will be exploring the festival of Diwali through The Story of Diwali by Malachy Doyle.
Science
Our science focus this term will be ‘forces and magnets’. We will start by learning about what a force is. Throughout the unit, children will develop their scientific enquiry skills by making predictions, carrying out fair tests, recording results, using evidence to draw conclusions, and communicating their findings.
Times tables
We use the Wiltshire Times Tables Challenge to teach times tables. It is taught throughout Key Stage 2 and used as an additional intervention in Years 4 and 5. The scheme focuses on teaching children 45 core times table facts and 21 ‘red’ facts, which are the 11x and 12x table facts and are taught towards the end of Year 4 (see below). From Term 4 of Year 2, children learn the 2x, 5x and 10x tables.
Core facts are those times tables that are frequently used in formal written methods of multiplication and division. As these are more regularly applied in other areas of maths, they are the main focus of times table teaching. The 11x and 12x table facts (red facts) are taught last, as they are not used when completing written methods of multiplication and can be derived if needed.
By developing a solid knowledge of times table facts, children are able to solve mathematical problems in other areas such as division, formal written methods, fractions, decimals, percentages and ratio. The overlearning aspects of times tables also enable children with special educational needs to retain facts better and access the same learning as their peers.
At the end of Year 4, children sit the Multiplication Check. This is a national test undertaken in June. The test is computer based and consists of 25 multiplication questions. Children have 6 seconds to answer each question. There is currently no official pass mark for this test. As a school, we have taken the decision to set 25 as our pass mark. Those children not achieving this by the end of Year 4 will receive an intervention in Year 5.
